lines: Biscuit just bowed to me. I bowed back. We are friends now.
Hello, Biscuit. Yes, I see the stick. It is a very good stick.
Biscuit is walking Yusuf again. Same time every afternoon.
Biscuit has found the one sunny paving stone. Of course he has.
Léo wants a dog exactly like Biscuit. Same ears, he says.
Biscuit sniffed my basket and approved of the peaches.
That terrier has better posture than anyone on the promenade.
A gull is standing on the fountain like he owns the place.
Two gulls sharing one lamp post. Very civilised.
That gull has been watching the café for an hour. Patient bird.
The gulls are doing slow circles. Afternoon is for slow circles.
A gull just landed beside me and looked at my book. Nosy.
Léo has named that gull Gérard. Gérard seems fine with it.
The ginger cat is on the wall again. Hello, Madame.
The wall cat has two speeds: asleep and slightly less asleep.
I stroked the cat on the wall. She allowed it. An honour.
The cat on the blue wall has moved six inches. With the sun.
That cat has the best seat in town and she knows it.
The cat and the gull are pretending not to see each other.
Chapter twelve, then I collect Léo. Possibly chapter thirteen.
My novel has a picnic in every chapter. I am reading it slowly.
Reading while walking. Léo says that is cheating. It is not.
I fold the corner of the page. Théo pretends not to see.
A good book, a warm wall, nowhere to be. The afternoon plan.
My book has a bakery on every page. It makes me hungry.
Henri lent me a book of poems. Every one is about lemons.
Odile has finished my crossword. Again. She leaves me one clue.
Eleven across, five letters, a calm afternoon. Siesta.
Henri gave me a crossword hint. It was another crossword clue.
Three clues left, and the sun is in no hurry either.
I do the crossword in pencil. Léo does it in crayon.
I am humming the café song. The one Marcel hums. Oh no.
The accordion man knows six songs. All of them lovely.
Léo whistled for the first time today. Mostly air. Very proud.
A radio in a window is playing old chansons. I slowed down.
Théo sings in the bath. Today I heard it from the promenade.
I am learning one song on the ukulele. One. It is enough.
My notebook of small moments is nearly full. Need a new one.
Small moment number four hundred: a gull with a croissant.
I press flowers from the walk. This one is a hollyhock.
Writing down Léo's best sentences. Today: the sea is shy.
I sketch the rooftops. They come out wonky. So are the real ones.
Drawing the fountain again. The fifth version has more pigeons.
My little watercolours make everything a touch too pink.
Afternoon loop: fountain, kiosk, the long way past the lemons.
I always go round the fountain twice. Once for me, once for luck.
Léo is at the fountain. I am at a respectful distance.
Léo, slower round the fountain! He is getting faster.
Léo just asked if fish have grandmothers. Good question.
Léo wants to know who switches the sun off. I said Marcel.
Léo is teaching his friend the rules. There are many rules.
Léo found a feather. He is now a gull, apparently.
Léo is practising his dancing for tonight. Very serious face.
Léo, socks are not for the fountain. Oh. Too late. Fine.
Théo has been on the same bench since lunch. Admirable.
Théo says strolling is a skill. He trains every afternoon.
Théo bought a second baguette. For the afternoon, he says.
Henri is watering the lemons. They look delighted, as always.
Henri tipped his hat. I curtsied. Nobody else saw. Lovely.
Odile waved from the bench. Odile always waves first.
Odile knows the cat's name. She knows everyone's name.
Lucie rang her bell twice. That means hello and also hurry.
Marcel is polishing the same glass and singing to it.
Marcel just shouted bravo at a pigeon. The pigeon bowed.
The shutters are half closed. The whole town is napping a bit.
Four o'clock. The light goes soft and so do I.
The plane trees are making little moving shadows. I follow them.
The afternoon smells of warm stone and somebody's tarte.
Everyone walks a little slower after lunch. Me included.
The cypresses look like they are standing very politely.
Washing on the line up the hill, like little flags.
The fountain is extra sparkly at this hour. I checked.
A bee is visiting every pot on the promenade. Thorough.
The kiosk has new postcards. I want all of them.
I bought a postcard of this exact view. While in this view.
An ice cream at four is not a snack. It is a tradition.
Pistachio for me, strawberry for Léo, both for Théo.
The lemonade at the kiosk is so cold it makes me laugh.
I bought peaches. Léo will eat three before supper.
Someone chalked a hopscotch by the fountain. I did one go.
A visitor asked me the way. I gave her the scenic version.
A little girl just told me my dress is the colour of the sea.
A visitor is photographing the cat. The cat is posing.
The neighbour from up the hill says the figs are early. Hooray.
Hats off the hooks, sun cream on noses. Afternoon rules.
Léo's shoes are untied. Léo's shoes are always untied.
I wore my good sandals for no reason. That is the reason.
My shopping list says bread. Théo has that covered. Twice.
Every afternoon I mean to sit. Every afternoon I wander.
Nothing happened this afternoon. It was wonderful.
The string lights are waiting for evening. So am I, a little.
Supper is soup. The walk is long. That is the deal.
If I stand very still, the town hums. Try it.
A bench, a page, a cat, a gull. Today has everything.
Henri held the gate for me. A gentleman, and a gate.
That breeze knows exactly where my neck is. Merci.
Four o'clock warmth. The kind you can wear like a cardigan.
I am walking slowly on purpose. It is allowed.
Someone swept the steps by the kiosk. Thank you, someone.
The jasmine is out again. I stop every single time.
Odile said my hat was lovely. I am keeping the hat forever.
A lemon fell at my feet. I put it back on Henri's wall.
Afternoons here are long and soft, like a good nap.
Léo's sandal strap, fixed with my hair clip. Motherhood.
The shade under the plane trees is two degrees of kindness.
I told Marcel his tarte was perfect. He bowed. Twice.
Théo carried my basket without being asked. Note it down.
I am collecting pink petals for Léo's collection. Very serious.
A little girl gave me a daisy. I gave her a whole smile.
Léo is dancing by the fountain. I pretend not to watch. I watch.
I found the bench with the best shade. I will share it.
The light is going honey-coloured at the edges. Not yet. Soon.
My phone is in my bag. My face is in the sun. Correct.
Every window box on this street is showing off today.
Henri offered me a lemon. I accepted with both hands.
Thank you, sun, for drying the washing before four.
The sea air is doing my hair a favour. Mostly.
I bought Léo a pencil at the kiosk. He will draw me a dog.
Léo held the door for a lady. I nearly burst.
I have walked past the same bougainvillea three times. On purpose.
The afternoon smells of fig leaves and sun cream.
Marcel waved a napkin at me. I waved my hat back.
Today's job: keep up with Léo. Today's result: almost.
Soft breeze, warm stones, one small boy humming. Perfect.
I promised Léo one more lap. He heard ten.
This is the hour the cats choose the best windowsills.
A neighbour waved from her balcony. I waved my whole arm.
A visitor thanked me for directions. I only said follow the jasmine.
Even the pigeons are strolling this afternoon.
Léo's best friend asked if I was the boss. I said, on Tuesdays.
The shop on the corner smells of lavender soap. I went in twice.
Hollyhocks, then roses, then the sea. The best walk in the world.
After you, said a gentleman. No, after you. We are still at the kiosk.
The light has gone all buttery on the white walls.
Henri complimented my walking pace. Unhurried, he said. High praise.
Léo gave his ice cream a lick and me the rest. Generous boy.
There is a breeze, then no breeze, then a better breeze.
Lucie brought us apricots from the market. Still warm.
Afternoon tea at home later. Afternoon sun right now.
Théo is somewhere with a baguette. I can tell by the gulls.
I am walking the long way home. It goes past the roses.
The fountain sounds sleepy at this hour. Me too, a little.
A boy dropped his marble. Léo ran it back to him. Proud.
The bakery girl said Léo has my smile. I said he has Théo's ears.
This warmth is the kind that makes everyone say bonjour.
My shadow is getting taller. Léo says so is he.
I picked up a lady's glove. She said merci like a song.
The awnings are out and every table has a view.
Odile has lent me her parasol. It has tassels. I feel royal.
I said thank you to the breeze. Out loud. Nobody minded.
One errand left: nothing. My favourite errand.
The palm fronds are clapping softly. For us, I think.
Léo is teaching his friend to dance. Lots of spinning.
A visitor asked for the best view. I pointed everywhere.
Warm stones under sandals. That is my whole summer.
Henri watered the roses and my sandals. Both are blooming.
The geraniums by the steps are new. Someone is very thoughtful.
Léo's favourite hour is four. Because of the snack.
I tucked a fig in Théo's pocket. A surprise for later.
The breeze turned my page for me. Helpful breeze.
The sky is that pale blue that goes with everything.
Léo said thank you to the kiosk man without a reminder. Bravo.
Afternoons like this, I forget what day it is. Lovely.
Little feet ahead of me, sun behind me. A good arrangement.
The bench under the cypress was still warm. Someone's gift.
Lucie fixed Léo's bike chain in a minute. Hero of the day.
I am wandering with intent. The intent is a lemon sorbet.
Even the string lights look relaxed in the daytime.
Léo found a feather and gave it to me. I am wearing it.
The waiter said I look rested. I said it is the town.
The sea is that sparkly kind today. Small diamonds everywhere.
Théo waved from the corner. I waved. Léo waved at both.
I am counting yellow shutters. Léo is counting cats.
A warm breeze off the water. Like the town is breathing out.
Odile's hydrangeas are blue this year. She is delighted.
Slow walk, warm air, sandy toes. I take it all, thank you.
Léo has done eleven laps of the fountain. He says ten.
Every child in town is orbiting the fountain. Little planets.
Wet sleeves, pink cheeks, one happy boy. A good afternoon.
Léo and his friend are racing the pigeons. The pigeons are winning.
Even the pavement looks pleased in this light.
A leaf is floating in the fountain. Léo named it Monsieur Duck.
I counted the laughs from the fountain. I lost count. Lovely.
I brought a book. I have read one page and watched the sky.
Léo wants to know why the fountain never gets tired.
The shadows are getting long and lazy. So am I.
Léo just showed a pigeon his shell. The pigeon was moved.
Somebody is playing piano with the window open. Merci, whoever.
A chalk sun on the pavement. Léo signed it, like a painter.
Is there anything nicer than nowhere to be at five o'clock?
Henri's lemons look like little suns. Everything is suns today.
Léo says the fountain sings if you listen closely. It does.
Damp shorts are a sign of a well-spent afternoon.
Léo is making wishes at the fountain. With buttons, not coins.
His friend fell in love with a snail. It now has a name. Bernard.
The cypresses are casting stripes across the square. Pretty.
A whole afternoon, a whole boy, a whole sky. Thank you, day.
Léo is hopping only on the white stones. Serious business.
My pocket is full of Léo's treasures. A pebble. A leaf. A grape.
Someone is watering geraniums upstairs. Little rain, just for them.
The fountain splashes, Léo squeals, the pigeons sigh.
Léo is drawing a map of the town. The fountain is enormous.
He wants to be a fountain when he grows up. Noted.
The kiosk man waved at me. I waved back with an ice cream.
Hide and seek behind the palms. Léo hides with his eyes shut.
Léo is counting the fountain spouts again. Always four.
Another mother and I share a bench and a smile. That is enough.
Three children, one ball, zero rules. Perfect game.
Léo wants a race to the lamp post. I will lose on purpose.
Léo's sandals are in my hand and his feet are in the sun.
A cartwheel from Léo! Well, most of a cartwheel. Bravo!
He is practising his bow for tonight. Very low. Very grand.
A cat asleep on a warm step. Nobody has the heart to move.
Léo splashes his friend. His friend splashes back. Everyone is happy.
A trail of wet footprints from the fountain. I know whose.
Léo picked me a dandelion. It is the best flower in France.
Léo wants to know how many drops are in the fountain. Many.
The plane trees whisper. I think they are gossiping about Théo.
Léo invented a game. The rules change every minute. He wins.
The little ones are feeding crumbs to the sparrows. Polite queue.
I am grateful for warm stone, cold lemonade and loud children.
Léo spun until he fell over laughing. Then he did it again.
Léo has a fountain beard of bubbles. Very distinguished.
The day is folding up slowly, like a good napkin.
Léo is walking backwards to see where we have been.
His friend asked me to hold a frog. It was a stone. I held it.
Late afternoon tastes of peaches. I have decided.
Léo stands on the fountain step and announces his name. Applause.
Léo whispered a secret into the fountain. It promised to keep it.
Odile's window has a vase of sunflowers in it. Every day, new ones.
Léo is lining up pebbles by size. A small museum.
Léo says he can see the moon already. He is right. Hello, moon.
A balloon went by on its way somewhere nice. We waved.
Sun on my shoulders, Léo's hand in mine. That is the whole list.
He fell asleep for one minute on the bench. Then: again!
Look at the light on the zinc roofs. Like spoons in a drawer.
Léo and his friend are building a fort of benches. Well, of one bench.
Every little window on the hill has a geranium. Who organised this?
Léo dipped his toes, then his knees. I stopped watching.
A quiet hour before bath time. I collect these.
Léo is drawing the fountain in chalk, life size. Ambitious.
Léo asked if the lamps are shy. They come on slowly, so yes.
Two little girls taught Léo a clapping song. He will sing it all week.
Léo gave the fountain a thumbs up. It splashed back. Friends.
If I could bottle five o'clock, I would keep it by the bed.
Léo wants to stay until the lights come on. That makes two of us.
Practising my pétanque throw. Mostly I hit the same palm tree.
Odile is teaching me her apricot jam. Step one: patience.
I am learning every cat's name. I am up to nine. And Mimi.
Learning a poem by heart for Léo. I have the first line. Twice.
Henri is showing me how to prune roses. Gently, he says. Always.
I can now juggle two lemons. Léo wants three. One day.
Practising my crêpe flip in my head. In real life, tomorrow.
Learning the waltz step for tonight. One, two, three, oops.
Lucie is teaching me to ride with one hand. She rings my bell for me.
I plaited the hair of Léo's friend. She asked for two plaits.
Practising a card trick for bath time. The card is always the queen.
A little book of bird calls. That one was a sparrow, I think.
Marcel taught me to carry three cups at once. I carried two. Bravo.
My paper bird looks like a happy croissant. Close enough.
Norwegian word of the day: takk. It means thank you. Takk, sun.
I am practising one-footed balance by the fountain. Léo too. Wobbly.
My calligraphy is improving. The letter C is my best. Camille.
I am learning the names of the flowers on this street. Hello, phlox.
Two-finger whistle, attempt nine. So far: a polite puff.
Henri says I am nearly ready to graft a lemon. Nearly is lovely.
Learning to make tarte tatin. Marcel says flip with confidence.
Learning to knit. Léo's scarf is now a very long wristband.
I practise my French tongue twisters on the gulls. They approve.
Practising a handstand against the wall. Léo is spotting me.
I am learning which hour the jasmine smells strongest. This one.
Learning to skim pebbles in the fountain. They just go plop. Cheerful.
Drawing hands today. Mine look like five little baguettes.
Lucie showed me how to fix a bike chain. I now have oily hands. Proud.
Practising my bow for the dance. Léo says lower, maman. Lower.
I am learning to tell the plane trees apart. That one is Albert.
Henri is teaching me lemon tree talk. You hum to them, it seems.
Practising patience while Léo ties his own shoes. Very good practice.
Learning to read the clouds. This one says ice cream at four.
Odile showed me how to press a hydrangea flat. It looks like lace.
Learning one magic word for every mood. Today's is merveilleux.
Practising the clapping song Léo learned. I am two claps behind.
Henri's lemonade has one secret: lots of stirring. I am stirring.
Practising a tiny pirouette when nobody looks. Marcel looked. Bravo.
A star book in my bag, ready for tonight. Hello, Vega.
I have learned that Léo laughs louder in the afternoon. Science.
Théo's grandmother's bread, attempt two. Flour everywhere.
Practising my sea swimming stroke on the promenade. Arms only.
Marcel is teaching me to fold napkins into swans. Mine is a duck.
This is where Léo took his very first steps. Right by this lamp.
Théo and I first met at that kiosk. He was buying two ice creams.
We had our wedding dance under these lights. Théo stepped on me once.
Moving day, Odile brought soup and a geranium. It still blooms.
Léo's first ice cream was right here. Pistachio. Everywhere.
The summer it rained one whole day, the town played cards in the café.
Henri gave Léo his first lemon. Léo carried it around for a week.
The whole town sang happy birthday to Léo. He hid. Then he bowed.
I remember the first time I saw this view. I said oh, out loud.
Théo asked me on that bench. With a lemon first, then a ring.
Léo said his first word on this street. It was pigeon.
The night of the festival, the fountain had candles all round it.
Lucie taught Léo to ride a bike by the kiosk. Everyone clapped.
My first walk here, a cat followed me home. Then went back. Polite.
Last spring we planted a tiny cypress. Now it is taller than Léo.
Léo once fell asleep in the ice cream queue. He kept his place.
I remember Marcel's first day. He sang then too.
The day the string lights first went up, everyone stayed out late.
Our first picnic here, a gull stole a single grape. Just the one.
This is the step where Léo found his first shell. Family history.
Odile taught me the crossword here. My first answer was sun.
The first summer, Théo learned to make coffee. It took all summer.
Every year we measure Léo by the fountain. Second spout now.
One afternoon the whole square danced to a radio. I still smile.
I wrote my first small-moment note on that bench. A gull, of course.
Léo once gave every neighbour a daisy. Even the cat.
Henri danced with me at our wedding. Very proper. Very twirly.
The day Léo was born, Marcel put a balloon on every table.
We once picnicked in the rain under Odile's parasol. Five of us.
This is the corner where Théo first held Léo's hand to cross.
I learned to love afternoons here. I used to rush. Not now.
Practising saying no to a second ice cream. Still practising.
Learning Léo's new dance. It involves a lot of being a gull.
My little sketchbook of memories is going to need a second shelf.
Practising patience with my watering can. Henri makes it look easy.
Léo can wink. I just blink very slowly. Charming, he says.
Seven shades of blue on the shutters so far. Still counting.
Practising my tarte crust with Odile. She says flaky is friendly.
Learning to sit still for a whole song. Théo is very encouraging.
I have learned the kiosk man's favourite flavour. Lemon. Of course.
Practising humming in harmony with the fountain. We are close.
A daisy chain long enough for Léo's head. Nearly there.
I practise remembering today, so I can tell Léo when he is grown.
Learning to fold a fitted sheet. Not today. Today is for walking.
Practising my handwriting on postcards. Dear Grand-mère, it is sunny.
Henri's trick: walk on the shady side, rest on the sunny side.
Léo is teaching me to count to ten in gull. It is all squawks.
Practising my best surprised face for Léo's next drawing.
Braiding lavender as I walk. The kitchen will smell wonderful.
I keep practising this walk. I think I have it perfect now.
First visit, I got lost by the cypresses. Best wrong turn of my life.
Tomorrow I repot the geraniums. Léo has asked to be foreman.
Henri's lemon tree glows under the lamp. Like a little lantern.
My mother had jasmine by the door. I smell it and I am six.
The night-scented stock is waking up. Just in time for us.
Plan for tomorrow: market, basil, one very small cactus for Léo.
Léo planted a sunflower seed in a yoghurt pot. We check daily.
Théo pours, I count the lemons on Henri's tree. Eleven.
The lavender by our step smells strongest when it gets blue.
Our wedding had bougainvillea on every table. Théo wore some.
Tomorrow, Léo wants to name the tomato plants. All of them.
A glass of rosé and the hibiscus closing up for the night.
My grandmother pressed flowers in her recipe book. I do too now.
Léo said goodnight to the basil. Then to the basil again.
Next week we plant a lemon tree of our own. Henri approves.
Santé to the roses. They had a big day.
Léo asked if flowers sleep. I said yes, in their pyjamas.
Tomorrow morning: watering can first, croissant second.
Théo proposed under a fig tree. It still gives us figs.
The blue hour makes every white wall look like milk.
Léo's sunflower is taller than his sock. A milestone.
The herb basket goes up tomorrow. Probably.
My father grew lemons in pots. He talked to them, like Henri.
The palms go dark first, then the cypresses. Then us.
Rosé the colour of the bougainvillea. Théo planned that.
Léo put a snail in the window box. It has a name: Gérard.
A quiet house, a cold glass, and the jasmine. Mm.
I like the hour when the geraniums turn the colour of jam.
Léo and I pick lavender tomorrow, for little bags. Gifts.
The pot by our door has mint, thyme and one surprised marigold.
When I was little we ate apricots straight from the tree.
Plan for Sunday: a picnic under the cypresses. Léo picks.
Léo drew our window box today. Seventeen flowers. We have four.
The string lights are on and the roses are taking a bow.
The hollyhocks get a stake tomorrow. They are reaching for Léo.
My sister sends seeds from the north. They grow very politely.
Léo is asleep with a petal in his pocket. I checked.
Odile says bougainvillea is a gossip. It gets into every garden.
One sip, one look at the sky, one look at the lemons.
We will dry the rose petals tomorrow. Léo has a jar ready.
The first time we came here, the jasmine was in bloom. We stayed.
The basil smells of tomorrow's lunch already.
Théo says the wine has notes of peach. I say notes of Théo.
Léo wants a lemon tree in his room. We are negotiating.
The fountain sounds softer once the flowers have closed.
Our first flat had one window and one geranium. We loved both.
The oleander and I have both earned a quiet evening.
Santé to the person who planted the first palm here.
Little plan: wake early, see the morning glories open.
Léo said the bougainvillea is pink paper. He is not wrong.
A cool glass and the smell of cut grass from the square.
The night lilies outside Odile's are just opening. Hello.
Léo's sunflower visits Henri tomorrow. Big outing.
Every window box on the street has its lamp now. So pretty.
Théo used to bring a gardenia on Fridays. Now Léo does too.
I could sit here until the jasmine is the only thing awake.
Tomorrow the basil gets a new pot. A blue one, Léo says.
Blue sky, pink glass, white walls, green leaves. A flag of us.
Henri watered our hydrangea too. It looks very spoiled.
We kept Léo's first shoes in a flowerpot. Now it grows chives.
The cypresses are tall black brushstrokes now. Lovely.
I picked one rose today and put it in a jam jar. It is enough.
My grandfather called this hour the garden's deep breath.
Léo's tomato has a tomato. One. We will share it three ways.
Théo and I are planning the garden. Mostly we plan the wine.
The geraniums on the balcony look like they are listening.
A breeze from the hills, smelling of thyme. Perfect timing.
Every summer, my aunt sent lavender honey. I still have a jar.
The bougainvillea is the last colour to fade. Brave thing.
To the window box. Four flowers, one snail, all thriving.
Plan for the weekend: paint the flowerpots. Léo has opinions.
When Léo was a baby, he slept best under the lemon tree.
The rosemary by the café smells best when nobody is looking.
Théo topped up my glass and tucked a sprig of thyme behind it.
The lamps make the oleander petals look like little moons.
Next spring, sweet peas. Léo wants them to climb to the roof.
My mother said: water at dusk, and the garden says thank you.
Santé, petit jardin. See you in the morning.
Léo is asleep and his marigold is asleep. Matching.
I will press a bougainvillea flower for Léo's school book.
The palm fronds are still against the sky. A good sign for tomorrow.
We met at a flower market. Théo bought tulips, then me a coffee.
Tomorrow, early: the hydrangea gets its drink before Henri can.
Blue hour, rosé hour. They are the same hour, really.
The lemon blossoms on Henri's tree smell like a holiday.
Léo planted a jelly bean. He expects a sweet tree by Tuesday.
Our street smells of jasmine and someone's supper. Bliss.
The garden is watered, the boy is asleep, the glass is full.
Tomorrow we visit the nursery up the hill. Léo is bringing a list.
I keep a lavender sprig in my pocket. Old family habit.
Léo is asleep. The fountain is now the loudest child in town.
Blue hour. Even my rosé looks a little bit blue.
The clock says ten past eight. It says it very kindly.
One glass, two chairs, zero bedtime stories left. Heaven.
Someone just closed their shutters. Click. Goodnight, number six.
A cat on the wall, watching the lamps come on one by one.
Théo is pretending to know about wine. He is very convincing.
The awnings are rolled up. The café is taking its hat off.
I read Léo three stories. I deserve this glass and a half.
The tiles are still warm. The whole street is a hot water bottle.
Santé to the duck. He did excellent work at bath time.
A gull on the clock tower. He thinks he tells the time.
Pink sky gone, blue sky here. The town changed outfits.
Biscuit just walked past like he owns the promenade. He might.
The fountain sounds different in the dark. Softer. Polite.
Every shutter on this street is a different blue. I counted.
My feet are up. My glass is up. Only the moon is higher.
That cat has not moved in an hour. A professional.
The church bell rang once. It knew we only needed one.
Henri and Odile on their bench. Same bench, same smile.
I left Léo's door open a crack. Exactly one crack wide.
Blue hour is my favourite colour. Do not tell the sunset.
Marcel brought olives without asking. A mind reader.
Even the gulls have gone quiet. Very considerate gulls.
The glass is cold, the evening is warm. A good pairing.
Lucie on the railing, Inès with her glass. Our evening regulars.
Théo says this is his third rosé. It is his second.
The kiosk shutter is down. Even newspapers need sleep.
Léo fell asleep holding the shell. The family treasure, on duty.
Terracotta pots, blue light. The colours are showing off.
A whole hour where nobody says Maman. Still, I listen for it.
We came out for one glass. The lamps convinced us to stay.
Théo toasted the baker. He is very loyal to bread.
Our window is the one with the little night light. See it?
The rosé is the colour of the sky an hour ago. Clever.
A moth is visiting each string light. Doing the rounds.
